speaker: ALEX
text: This is Git Going with GitHub, episode 44: Choose Your Tools. I'm Alex, and today we're walking through five different ways to work with GitHub.

speaker: JAMIE
text: I'm Jamie. I'll be asking the questions that come up: What's this for? Where am I right now? How do I know it actually worked?

speaker: ALEX
text: Here's what matters today: There isn't one right way to use GitHub. Some developers switch between the browser, github.dev, VS Code, GitHub Desktop, and the CLI depending on what they're doing. Our job is to show you each environment, explain what's possible in each one, and help you figure out which one fits your workflow.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So this should work as a standalone guide, even if someone hasn't read the chapter yet.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. We name the concept, explain why it matters, walk through the move, and point out the checks that let you verify it worked.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What's the landscape here?

speaker: ALEX
text: Five environments. GitHub.com in the browser is your foundation--every repository, issue, pull request, and setting lives there. github.dev is VS Code running in the browser, so you can edit files without installing anything. VS Code is the full desktop editor with Git built in, thousands of extensions, and Copilot. GitHub Desktop is a graphical Git client for clone, branch, commit, and push operations. And the GitHub CLI lets you do all of that from your terminal.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Why does the workshop teach all five instead of just saying, "use this one"?

speaker: ALEX
text: Because different people need different tools based on their workflow, their equipment, and their accessibility needs. Some work better in the browser. Others need a full code editor. Someone using a screen reader might prefer the CLI or VS Code over the graphical interface. The key is knowing what you can do in each environment and what you can't, so you can make the choice that works for you.

speaker: ALEX
text: Let's start with Path 1: GitHub.com. It's the website at github.com--every repository, issue, pull request, and setting is there.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What's possible from here?

speaker: ALEX
text: You can browse repositories, files, and folders. Create, comment on, and close issues. Open, review, and merge pull requests. Edit individual files using the pencil icon. Manage labels, milestones, and project boards. And configure repository settings.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And the limits?

speaker: ALEX
text: You can't run code or tests locally. You don't have a full-featured code editor with extensions. And you can't make changes if you're offline. But here's what matters: for screen reader users, GitHub.com has strong support. Every page uses ARIA landmarks, headings follow a consistent hierarchy, and keyboard shortcuts are available for most actions. You can press S to jump to search, D to navigate between landmark regions, or G then I to jump to Issues. If you're using low vision settings, GitHub supports light and dark themes, high contrast options, and responds to your system's contrast preferences. You can zoom up to 400% on most pages without horizontal scrolling.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How do I verify I'm in the right place?

speaker: ALEX
text: Before you do anything, know where you are. Check the headings, use ARIA landmarks to orient yourself, and check the address bar. Link underlines in the Accessibility settings help distinguish links by more than just color. High contrast themes are at github.com/settings/appearance. Browser zoom above 200% collapses the repository sidebar into a menu, so keep that in mind if you're working at higher zoom levels.

speaker: ALEX
text: Now let's look at github.dev. It's VS Code running entirely in your browser.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How do I access it?

speaker: ALEX
text: Press the period key on any GitHub repository page, or change the URL from github.com to github.dev. You can also type github.dev/ followed by the repository path.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What can I do there?

speaker: ALEX
text: Edit multiple files with a file explorer, tabs, and a terminal preview. View file diffs and stage changes. Commit directly to a branch. Use many VS Code extensions that run in the browser. You can even use the command palette--Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P--and all the editor keybindings work the same way.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What can't I do?

speaker: ALEX
text: You can't run code or build projects--the terminal is read-only for Git operations. You can't use extensions that need a local runtime, like debuggers or compiled tools. And you can't work offline, though your changes stay in the browser until you commit them.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Screen reader and low vision support?

speaker: ALEX
text: github.dev is VS Code in the browser, so the same keyboard navigation and screen reader support applies. The command palette works, all editor keybindings are available, and the accessibility support is solid.

speaker: JAMIE
text: When do I choose github.dev over GitHub.com?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use github.dev when you need to edit more than one file in a single commit, or when you want the code editor experience without installing anything. For a single-file edit, the pencil icon on GitHub.com is simpler.

speaker: ALEX
text: Path 3 is VS Code on your desktop. It's a free code editor from Microsoft with built-in Git support, an integrated terminal, thousands of extensions, and GitHub Copilot included.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What's the capability here?

speaker: ALEX
text: Edit files with full IntelliSense, syntax highlighting, and extension support. Use the integrated terminal to run Git commands, scripts, and programs. Stage, commit, push, and pull using the Source Control panel or the terminal. Run and debug code. Use Copilot for suggestions, chat, and code review. Work offline--Git operations sync when you reconnect.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Limitations?

speaker: ALEX
text: You can't manage issues and pull requests directly without installing the GitHub Pull Requests extension. You can't view repository insights or settings--use GitHub.com for that.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Accessibility features?

speaker: ALEX
text: VS Code has a dedicated accessibility mode that activates automatically when a screen reader is detected. The Accessibility Help dialog opens with Alt+F1 or Option+F1 in any view, and all panels are reachable via keyboard shortcuts. For low vision users, there are high contrast themes, custom zoom levels--Ctrl+= to zoom in, Ctrl+- to zoom out--and configurable font sizes. You can disable the minimap if it's distracting: open the command palette, type minimap, and toggle the setting off.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How do I get oriented in VS Code?

speaker: ALEX
text: Press Ctrl+Shift+E to focus the File Explorer. Use Up and Down arrows to navigate, Enter to open a file, and Right arrow to expand a folder. Press Ctrl+Shift+G to focus Source Control, and the changed files list announces each file's Git status. The theme picker is Ctrl+K Ctrl+T--"High Contrast" and "High Contrast Light" offer the strongest differentiation. And if you zoom repeatedly with Ctrl+=, the zoom level persists after restart.

speaker: ALEX
text: Path 4 is GitHub Desktop. It's a graphical Git client that handles clone, branch, commit, and push operations without touching the terminal.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What can I do with it?

speaker: ALEX
text: Clone repositories with one click. Create, switch, and merge branches. View file diffs in side-by-side or unified view. Stage individual files or specific lines within a file. Commit with a message and push to GitHub. You can also open pull requests, though that launches GitHub.com.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What can't I do?

speaker: ALEX
text: You can't edit code--GitHub Desktop is a Git client, not an editor. It opens your preferred editor when you need to make changes. You can't review pull requests with inline comments, and you can't manage issues, labels, or project boards.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How accessible is it?

speaker: ALEX
text: GitHub Desktop uses Electron and provides basic screen reader support. Branch switching, commit history, and file lists are navigable. For a more detailed walkthrough of the interface, that's covered in Appendix H.

speaker: JAMIE
text: When would I choose this over VS Code?

speaker: ALEX
text: When you want a visual Git workflow without the overhead of a full code editor. Or when you prefer graphical diffs and staging over the command line.

speaker: ALEX
text: Path 5 is the GitHub CLI. It's a command-line tool that lets you do everything from the terminal.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What can I do?

speaker: ALEX
text: Clone repositories, create branches, stage and commit changes, push to GitHub, open pull requests, and manage issues. You can chain commands together and automate workflows. You can also view repository data in formats like JSON or CSV, which is useful for scripting.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What can't I do?

speaker: ALEX
text: You can't edit files directly with the CLI--you'll use your preferred editor for that. You can't view visual diffs or graphical commit histories the way GitHub Desktop does.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Accessibility?

speaker: ALEX
text: The CLI works well with screen readers because it's text-based. You hear each command's output, error messages are clear, and keyboard navigation is straightforward. For detailed examples and command reference, see Appendix I.

speaker: JAMIE
text: When would I pick the CLI?

speaker: ALEX
text: When you're already working in the terminal and want to stay there. When you want to automate workflows with scripts. When you prefer text-based output over graphical interfaces. Or when you're comfortable with command syntax and want maximum control.

speaker: ALEX
text: So which path should you start with?

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's say I'm brand new.

speaker: ALEX
text: Start with GitHub.com. You can browse, create issues, review pull requests, and edit single files--all without installing anything. Get comfortable with the concepts and the interface before you add tools.

speaker: JAMIE
text: After that?

speaker: ALEX
text: Move to github.dev or VS Code, depending on whether you want to install software. github.dev is the bridge--same editor experience, but in the browser. VS Code is the full workshop--once you're ready for that, you get a terminal, extensions, debugging, and Copilot.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What about switching between them?

speaker: ALEX
text: It's normal. You might use GitHub.com for quick edits and issue work, then switch to VS Code for larger changes. You might use GitHub Desktop for branch work and the CLI for scripting. The workflow stays the same--you're still cloning, committing, and pushing. The tool just changes.

speaker: ALEX
text: Let's do a confidence exercise. The task: Clone the repository, find the README, and read the first paragraph.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Show me the GitHub.com path first.

speaker: ALEX
text: Go to github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github. The file list appears. Find README.md and click it. You're done when the file content appears. The key is: you didn't clone anything. You just browsed to the file. That's the difference between GitHub.com and the other tools.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Now github.dev.

speaker: ALEX
text: Go to github.dev/Community-Access/git-going-with-github. Press Ctrl+Shift+E to focus the file explorer. Navigate to README.md and press Enter. You're done when the file content appears in the editor. The difference here is you have tabs, a terminal preview, and syntax highlighting--but you still haven't downloaded the repository.

speaker: JAMIE
text: VS Code?

speaker: ALEX
text: Open VS Code. Press Ctrl+Shift+P, type Git: Clone, and press Enter. Paste the URL: https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github.git. Choose a folder to clone into. When it finishes, accept the offer to open the repository. Press Ctrl+Shift+E and select README.md. You're done when the file appears in the editor. This time you downloaded the whole repository.

speaker: JAMIE
text: GitHub Desktop?

speaker: ALEX
text: Open GitHub Desktop. Press Ctrl+Shift+O or go to File, then Clone repository. Paste the URL: https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github.git. Choose a local path and click Clone. Once cloned, the repository appears in the list. Click "Open in Visual Studio Code" or your preferred editor. You're done when you can read the README. Again, you downloaded the whole repository.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And the CLI?

speaker: ALEX
text: Open your terminal. Type: gh repo clone Community-Access/git-going-with-github. Then: cd git-going-with-github. Then: cat README.md to print it to the terminal, or code README.md to open it in VS Code. You're done when you can read the first paragraph. Same outcome--you downloaded the repository and found the file.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What's the point of all those different paths?

speaker: ALEX
text: They're all valid. The question is: which one fits how you work? Do you prefer a graphical interface or the terminal? Are you offline or online? Do you need extensions and debugging, or just a simple editor? Do you have accessibility needs that point you toward one tool or another? There's no wrong answer. There's only the answer that works for you today.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What if someone gets stuck?

speaker: ALEX
text: Start with Chapter 02: Understanding GitHub. It covers the foundational concepts behind all five paths. If you're working with GitHub Desktop, see Appendix H. If you're using the CLI, see Appendix I. If you're interested in Codespaces--that's a cloud-based development environment--see Appendix J.

speaker: ALEX
text: Here's what to carry with you: Know what page or tool you're in. Know which action you're about to take. Know what confirmation should follow. If that confirmation is missing, pause. That pause isn't wasted time--it's how you keep control of the workflow.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That makes it less about following instructions and more about understanding what's happening.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Steps matter, but understanding wins. That's episode 44. Next is episode 45, where we keep building the same contributor skills. We'll see you there.
